title: Companionable solitude
hookLine: Thoreau never found a companion so companionable as solitude
carry: solitude can be company, not loneliness

cards: A rainy evening. No visitors. The nearest neighbor is a long walk away.

For some people, that's a picture of loneliness. For Thoreau, in the fifth chapter of Walden, it's something close to good company. He calls the chapter Solitude, and he says, without apology, that he enjoyed being alone.
More than that: solitude was the best companion he'd found. Some readers find that sentence beautiful, and others find it a little suspicious. It's worth listening to carefully.

teach.b: First, the sentence: "I never found the companion that was so companionable as solitude." Companion and companionable, side by side, on purpose. In this line, solitude isn't the absence of company.
It is company, and of a good kind.
Second, the surprise: "We are for the most part more lonely when we go abroad among men than when we stay in our chambers." Loneliness, he suggests, isn't about how many people are near.
You can feel it at a crowded party and be free of it in an empty room.
Solitude, he says, isn't measured in the miles between people. Third, the rain. Thoreau is honest that it wasn't always easy.
Early on, for an hour, he wondered whether he needed people nearby to live well.

teach.h: A KINDLY SOCIETY IN THE RAIN.
teach.b: Then, in a gentle rain, he felt suddenly aware of a sweet and kindly society in nature itself, in the pattering of the drops and every sound around his house. The loneliness passed and didn't return.

Fourth, the joke: "I have a great deal of company in my house; especially in the morning, when nobody calls." It's funny, and exact. When nobody calls, there's room for the morning, the pond and his own thoughts.
His solitude was never total: he walked into town, and friends came by. But being alone, for him, was something to be glad of, not something to be cured.

how: Some readers of Walden set aside regular time alone, walking or sitting quietly, and treat it as company rather than as loneliness, after the Solitude chapter.

games.q: you're alone in a cabin on a rainy evening, and for an hour you wonder if you need people nearby. what happens to Thoreau?
o: he packs up and goes back to town.
in the pattering rain, he feels a sweet society in nature.
he invites the whole village over.
games.why: he says he was suddenly aware of a sweet and kindly society in nature, in the very pattering of the drops, and the loneliness passed.

practice: For these two minutes nobody needs anything from you, and you don't need anything from anybody; notice what it's like to be your own company, restful or restless, either is fine.
Then see if you can treat yourself the way Thoreau treated the rain, as company worth keeping. Let there be a little warmth toward the one who is sitting here.
